findings.title: Expiry check is unreachable dead code, never enforced first (or at all) for privileged/owner paths
findings.finding: The requirement mandates that an expired grant deny export before any role or ownership check, including for administrators. The implementation does the opposite: role and ownership checks happen first and return True unconditionally, so the expiry check on line 9 is only reached when the actor is neither admin/auditor nor the owner — and in that remaining branch both the true and false outcomes of the expiry test return False anyway. This makes the expiry check functionally dead code: an expired grant never denies an admin, auditor, or matching owner, directly violating the ordering and coverage the policy requires.

An expired grant therefore exports for administrators, auditors, and matching owners.
access_policy.py:5-6 `if role in {"admin","auditor"}: return True` executes before any expiry check, so expired admin/auditor access is granted.
access_policy.py:7-8 owner match returns True before the expiry check on line 9, so an expired owner grant is still permitted.
access_policy.py:9-11 both branches of the expiry test return False, so this code has no observable effect on the function's output regardless of expires_at.
missing_tests: Expired grant for admin, auditor, matching owner, and non-owner member.
Expired grant + role=admin/auditor must assert can_export(...) is False
Expired grant + matching owner_id/actor_id must assert can_export(...) is False
Non-expired grant + matching owner must still assert True after fixing ordering

findings.title: Auditor role incorrectly bypasses export like admin, violating inspect-only restriction
findings.finding: Per the policy, only administrators may bypass ownership; auditors may inspect but must never export. The implementation groups 'admin' and 'auditor' into the same unconditional bypass set, so an auditor actor is granted export rights identically to an admin, with no distinction and no expiry/ownership check at all. This is a direct authorization-bypass defect for the auditor role.
evidence: access_policy.py:5 returns True for both admin and auditor without checking ownership or expiry.
This allows auditors to export, contrary to the requirement that only administrators may bypass ownership and auditors never export.

No branch anywhere in access_policy.py restricts auditor to a non-export ('inspect') capability; the function only returns a boolean export decision.
verify.py has no test asserting `not can_export(..., 'auditor', ...)`, so this bypass is unverified and unguarded.

Member may export only an unexpired owned record.

can_export for role='admin' on a non-owned record must assert True (admin ownership bypass permitted)
can_export for role='member' (non-owner) must assert False

findings.title: Owner ID comparison uses case-insensitive casefold(), violating case-sensitive opaque identifier requirement
findings.finding: The policy specifies owner IDs are case-sensitive opaque identifiers. The implementation normalizes both sides with `.casefold()` before comparing, making the match case-insensitive. This allows an actor whose ID differs only in case from the true owner (e.g., 'Acct-1' vs 'acct-1') to be treated as the owner and granted export, which is a real identity-comparison defect for opaque IDs that must be compared byte-for-byte.
evidence: access_policy.py:7 compares owner_id and actor_id using casefold().
Case variants such as acct-1 and ACCT-1 are treated as equal, although owner IDs are case-sensitive opaque identifiers.
access_policy.py:7 `if owner_id.casefold() == actor_id.casefold(): return True` performs case-insensitive comparison.
verify.py:2 only tests exact-case equal IDs ('acct-1' vs 'acct-1'), so the case-insensitivity defect is not exercised or caught.
No test in verify.py supplies differing-case IDs (e.g., 'Acct-1' vs 'acct-1') to confirm they should NOT match.
missing_tests: Owned record with exact-case IDs is allowed.
IDs differing only by case are denied.

owner_id and actor_id identical exact-case strings must assert True (regression guard)
owner_id/actor_id with case-differing but otherwise identical opaque tokens containing mixed-case UUIDs

findings.title: Expiry comparison uses naive datetime.now(), not timezone-aware UTC, risking crashes or silent misbehavior
findings.finding: The policy requires expiry timestamps to be timezone-aware UTC. The implementation compares `expires_at` against `datetime.now()`, which returns a naive local-time datetime with no tzinfo. If callers pass a timezone-aware `expires_at` (as required), comparing it to a naive `datetime.now()` raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, crashing the function. If callers pass a naive `expires_at` instead, the comparison silently uses local time rather than UTC, producing incorrect expiry decisions across timezones/DST. Either way this violates the UTC timezone-aware requirement.
evidence: access_policy.py:9 compares expires_at with datetime.now(), which is timezone-naive and local-time based.
A timezone-aware expiry raises TypeError during comparison; naive expiry evaluation is not explicitly UTC-based.
access_policy.py:9 `expires_at <= datetime.now()` — `datetime.now()` is naive (no tzinfo), never UTC-aware.
access_policy.py:1 only imports `datetime`, never `timezone`; there is no `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` usage anywhere in the module.
verify.py never passes an `expires_at` value (all three calls use `None`), so this naive/aware mismatch is completely untested.
missing_tests: Aware UTC expiry before and after now.
Aware non-UTC expiry representing the same instant.
Naive expiry must be rejected or handled explicitly without TypeError.
expires_at = timezone-aware UTC datetime in the past must assert can_export is False without raising TypeError
expires_at = timezone-aware UTC datetime in the future must assert can_export True path is unaffected by expiry
Mixing naive expires_at with aware 'now' comparator (or vice versa) should assert a defined error or normalized behavior, not silent local-time drift

findings.title: verify.py relies solely on bare `assert` statements, which are stripped under optimized interpreter mode (-O)
findings.finding: verify.py's only validation mechanism is three top-level `assert` statements. Under CPython's optimized mode (`python -O` or `-OO`), assert statements are compiled to no-ops and silently skipped, so the script would exit with code 0 having performed zero checks — giving false confidence that the policy is correct. The host's stated acceptance command (`python -B verify.py`) does not pass `-O`, so it currently executes correctly, but the verifier is not robust to optimized interpreter invocation and contains no explicit failure reporting, exit-code checks, or protection against assertion stripping.
evidence: verify.py:2-4 contains only three assert statements and omits expiry, auditor, case-sensitivity, and timezone checks.
Running the host verifier with normal and optimized modes both exits 0; under -O, Python removes all assert statements, so no checks execute.
verify.py:2-4 use bare `assert can_export(...)` / `assert not can_export(...)` with no accompanying non-assert validation logic.
Python semantics: `assert` statements are removed from bytecode when `__debug__` is False (i.e., under `-O`/`-OO`), so `python -O verify.py` would run with no checks performed and no error raised.
verify.py contains no `if __debug__` guard, no manual `if not cond: raise SystemExit(1)` fallback, and no summary/exit-code confirmation of how many checks ran.
missing_tests: Execute the full policy checks under both normal and -O modes and require failures to remain observable.
Run verify.py under `python -O verify.py` and confirm it still fails/reports when can_export is broken (currently it would pass silently)
Add a non-assert-based check (e.g., explicit if/raise or unittest) so failures are detected regardless of interpreter optimization flags
Add a final print/exit-code confirmation of number of assertions executed to detect a no-op run

findings.title: Expiry check is subordinate to role/owner checks and functionally dead
findings.finding: The requirement mandates that an expired grant deny export before any role or ownership check, including for administrators. The implementation instead checks role first (line 5-6) and owner (line 7) before ever touching expires_at (line 9), so admins/auditors and matching owners bypass expiry entirely. Worse, even when the expiry branch is reached, both the true and false paths of the if-statement return False, so the expires_at value never actually changes the outcome for anyone — the expiry logic is dead code rather than an enforced precedence rule.
